name: Dreierles (Baden Tarock)
description: Dreierles (also known as Dreierle or Dreier) is a sophisticated trick-taking game from the Baden region of Germany, played with a 54-card Cego (Tarot) deck. It belongs to the Tarock family and is closely related to Austrian Tapp Tarock. In Dreierles, a single declarer plays against a team of opponents, utilizing a six-card 'blind' (talon) from which they draw exactly three cards to improve their hand, giving the game its name.

content.text: Dreierles (also known as Dreierle or Dreier) is a sophisticated trick-taking game from the Baden region of Germany, played with a 54-card Cego (Tarot) deck. It belongs to the Tarock family and is closely related to Austrian Tapp Tarock. In Dreierles, a single declarer plays against a team of opponents, utilizing a six-card 'blind' (talon) from which they draw exactly three cards to improve their hand, giving the game its name.

Dreierles survived as a niche tradition in central Baden (around Rastatt) alongside the better known Cego. It likely shares an ancestor with 19th-century Austrian Tarock variants, possibly imported during the era of the Austrian garrisons in the Rastatt federal fortress.
Usually 3 players. If 4 play, the dealer sits out the hand.
54-card Cego pack. Consists of 22 Tarocks (Trumps), 16 Court cards (K, Q, C, J), and 16 pip cards (Leere).
Each player receives 16 cards (in batches of 4). 6 cards are dealt face-down to the center to form the 'Blind' (Talon).

items.text: Steinmauern tournament: No knocking; Räuber 3 or 4 points; penalty 3 for incorrect deal, 8×bid factor for illegal play; rounds set by organiser.
Iffezheim: Different terminology (Alt, Eisen, Pfiff); 4-player: only active players score, dealer cannot knock in Räuber; only declarer scores combinations; Räuber play restrictions on Drull cards.
Achertal: Solo Du bid (win all 16 tricks, no blind); scoring as positive/negative points; Kleiner Mann am Schluss; Ramsch for all-pass; 4 active players get 12 cards each.
